#10003. No Effect Before Its Cause: From Einstein to Lamport

Causality in collaborative editors · Part 1 of 2

Einstein's moving train, Leslie Lamport's clocks and a 2,500-year-old idea explain the core problem of leaderless replication: ordering writes when no clock can be trusted.

When developers explain what happens when two computers communicate, there's a very high chance Alice and Bob get involved, and I'm not going to break tradition.

Once upon a time there was a boy called Bob and a girl called Alice. Their school gives them a literature homework assignment, and since they live too far from each other to meet up, they decide to do it in Notion, a collaborative document tool. Now both of them are editing the same document at the same time. So far it says "That flower", and Alice adds "is pretty" to the end of it.

Just before Alice's edit reaches him, Bob's internet connection drops, and he doesn't notice. A few minutes later, still unaware of her edit, he types "shall I pick it?" in the same spot. Then his connection comes back, and his edit finally syncs.

Now Notion has a big problem: it has to figure out what the sentence says. The obvious rule is "newest timestamp wins": Bob's clock says he typed later, so "shall I pick it?" stays and "is pretty" quietly disappears, even though Bob never saw it. That is a lost update, and it's one of the central problems of leaderless replication, where every copy of the data accepts writes on its own and no almighty entity decides the order.

Before you read: the rest of the article runs from Einstein's train to Lamport's clocks, ending at CRDTs. If you don't want the physics, skip the train and start at Lamport's clocks. If you want neither the physics nor the computer science history, jump straight to what leaderless replication means. And if leaderless replication is already familiar and you only want to know how CRDTs work, skip all of this and continue to the next article: Part 2: how Yjs pulls this off.

So how did programmers solve it? It turns out that before computers even existed, physicists ran into this exact problem more than a century ago.

In 1905, a 26-year-old patent clerk named Albert Einstein realised something unsettling: two events can be simultaneous for one person and not simultaneous for another, and both people are right. In 1916, he explained it with a train.

Picture a train zooming along a track. Lightning strikes both ends of it. A woman is standing on the platform, exactly halfway between the two strikes. Both flashes reach her at the same moment, so she says: "Simultaneous. Obviously."

The catch is that light doesn't add up like a thrown ball. Throw a ball forward on a moving train and someone on the platform sees it go faster, because the train's speed adds to the throw. Light travels at the same speed for everyone, moving or not.

Now the man sitting in the middle of the train. While the light is travelling, the train carries him toward the front flash and away from the rear one, so the front flash reaches him first. Both flashes travel at the same speed, and he's sitting exactly in the middle of the train. So, as far as he's concerned, the flash that reaches him first must have happened first. He says: "The front strike happened first."

So, whose perspective is correct? Both of them. There is no master clock hanging over the universe to tell either of them they're wrong. "At the same time" is not a fact about the universe. It's a fact about whoever is watching. Einstein basically invented "it depends," and programmers have been billing for it ever since, and hopefully will for the foreseeable future.

This is exactly the problem with comparing timestamps from two servers. Every server's clock is its own little train. Clocks drift, jump, and get corrected by NTP (the network time protocol that keeps server clocks roughly in sync) at the worst possible moment. Asking "whose edit came first?" by comparing clocks is like asking the woman on the platform and the man on the train to agree on which strike came first. Each has their own point of view, so they won't agree.

So if nobody agrees on when, does anyone agree on anything? Yes: cause and effect. If the first flash lit a fuse that set off the second, every observer, on any platform or any train, sees the cause before the effect. People can argue about timing all day, but an effect can never show up before its cause.

Take any event, like a firework going off. Light spreads out from it in every direction, and nothing in the universe is faster than light, with the possible exception of bad news. That growing bubble of light splits all of spacetime into three zones:

Quick example: two points on opposite sides of the Earth are about 12,700 km apart in a straight line through the planet, so even light needs about 42 milliseconds to connect them (and about 67 ms if it had to follow the surface, the way a cable does). Two events there one second apart could be causally linked. Ten milliseconds apart? No signal could connect them, so asking which came first has no physical answer.

Now, how computer scientists stumbled onto the same problem.

In 1978, Leslie Lamport looked at a network of computers and thought, "This is basically a tiny universe." Every machine was an observer with its own clock, and there was no master clock to settle arguments. His paper, "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System," borrows its central idea straight from special relativity.

He draws the network as a simple picture. Each computer is a vertical line, with time running along it. When one computer sends a message to another, you draw an arrow from the sender's line to the receiver's line. The arrow slants because the message takes time to travel: it leaves at one moment and lands at a later one. Messages are the light rays of this universe. They are the only way one machine can find out what another machine did.

Read it by following the arrows. Even though c1 sits between a1 and a2 on the page, no chain of arrows connects them, so they are concurrent, whatever any clock says.

From that picture, Lamport defined happens-before, and notice that it never mentions a clock.

If neither happens before the other, the events are concurrent. They're in each other's elsewhere. Martin Kleppmann sums it up in Designing Data-Intensive Applications: two operations are concurrent when neither knows about the other, no matter what the clock said. Concurrency isn't about doing things at the same time. It's about being clueless at the same time.

The physics here is an analogy, and it breaks in one place. Light has a fixed speed limit, so physics can say exactly what could have affected what. A network has no such limit. What counts is whether a message actually arrived, so two edits made an hour apart can still be concurrent if a connection dropped in between.

Now we can say exactly what went wrong during Bob's network outage. By the wall clock, Bob typed minutes after Alice. But wall-clock order is not cause-and-effect order. The key fact is this: Bob never saw "is pretty." His edit lives in Alice's elsewhere, so the two edits are concurrent. Neither came first, so neither should win just because of what a clock says.

Here's the whole drama, drawn the way Lamport would draw it. Each vertical line is a replica moving through time, and each arrow is a message.

No chain of arrows connects Alice's edit to Bob's, in either direction. They're strangers in the elsewhere. The minutes between them on the wall clock say nothing about cause and effect.

In practice, leaderless means there's no single source of truth everyone has to bow to. Every replica (each copy of the data, on each server or device) accepts writes on its own, online or offline, and the replicas swap updates afterwards. Databases like Amazon's Dynamo, Riak and Cassandra work this way, and so do many collaborative editors. Even when an editor has a sync server in the middle, it's just a messenger relaying updates, not a judge. The goal is that once every replica has received the same updates, they all hold exactly the same data.

That sounds easy until two replicas accept conflicting writes and something has to decide which came first.

This is the central problem of leaderless replication. When any replica can accept writes at any time, with no leader deciding the order, concurrent writes like Bob's and Alice's are guaranteed to happen, and every leaderless system has to decide what to do with them.

There are three common answers. The first trusts clocks. The other two stay on the relativity road and run on cause and effect.

Give every write a timestamp and keep the one with the latest. Cassandra does this by default. It's simple, and it's exactly the mistake Einstein and Lamport taught us to avoid. Bob's clock says "later," so "shall I pick it?" wins and "is pretty" silently disappears, even though Bob never saw it. In the worst case, if one replica's clock runs fast, its writes can beat writes that really came after them. Last write wins doesn't resolve conflicts. It hides them.

This is the approach used by Amazon's Dynamo and databases like Riak. Each version of the data carries a version vector: a small set of counters, one per replica, recording which updates that version has already seen. If neither version has seen everything the other has, they're concurrent. The database then keeps both versions side by side (Riak calls them siblings) and lets the application merge them.

Story time: back in 2007, Amazon's cart had a problem, and it has documented in the Dynamo paper. Amazon wanted "add to cart" to always work, even when the network was having a bad day, so any replica could accept a write. That means two replicas can end up with different carts. One has a book. Another, which never heard about the book, has a phone. Dynamo used version vectors (it called them vector clocks) to notice that the two carts were concurrent, and it kept both. The application then merged them by taking the union: now the cart has the book and the phone. Nothing you added is ever lost. The price is that a deleted item can sometimes come back from the dead.

Read it top to bottom: the database never picks a winner. It keeps both carts as siblings, and the next write merges them.

The third answer is the CRDT, short for conflict-free replicated data type. It's a data structure built so that replicas that have seen the same updates always end up with the same result, with nobody stepping in to decide. There are no siblings, and no merge code for you to write.

The trick is that a CRDT never stores "put this word at position 5," because position 5 means different things on different replicas once edits start flying around. Instead it relies on three ideas:

For Bob and Alice, that means both words survive. Their two inserts claim the same spot, so every replica falls back on a tie-break rule they all share, something deterministic like "lower replica ID goes first." Same data plus same rule gives the same order everywhere, with no one having to coordinate. And because of how the rules are built, updates can arrive in any order, arrive twice, or arrive late, and the result doesn't change: same set of updates in, same document out.

Collaborative editing libraries like Yjs and Automerge are built on CRDTs, and Riak offers CRDT data types too.

Part 2 of this article goes deep on this third approach using Yjs, a JavaScript library for collaborative editing, because it's the one I have actual experience with. That experience comes from the work of Tharaka Ariyarathna, an absolute legend, whose Notion-like collaborative editor for a customer success management (CSM) platform pulled me into this rabbit hole.

Read it here: Part 2: how Yjs pulls this off with a handful of bytes per character.

It's a mouthful (roughly: pruh-TEE-tyuh-sum-oot-PAH-duh). It's a Buddhist idea usually translated as dependent origination, and its shortest form goes: when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.

I'm not a Buddhist scholar, just as I'm not a physicist, so I'm borrowing the idea very loosely. In the suttas it's mostly about how suffering arises, not about ordering database writes. Please don't send either profession after me.

Still, it rhymes with this article. Bob's and Alice's edits are concurrent because neither caused the other, so neither has to wait for the other. But some updates do depend on an earlier one. Say Bob reads "is pretty" and replies by typing "too" right after it. His insert says "put me right after alice:3", which is Alice's edit. If that update reaches a replica before Alice's does, the replica has nothing for it to point at. A CRDT doesn't freak out and declare the universe broken, and it doesn't guess a position either. It holds Bob's update in a queue until alice:3 arrives, then applies it. When this exists, that comes to be; until then, the update sits patiently in the queue.

You never see a glass shatter before it falls. A CRDT works the same way: an update never takes effect before the one it depends on, however confused the clocks are. Some things come before other things because one caused the other, and no clock has to agree for that to be true.

To be continued: how Yjs actually pulls this off, with origins, YATA and state vectors. Read Part 2: Yjs Internals →

#10002. To thwart reverse engineering by agents, dev proposes blinding them

Now that LLMs can help analyze commercial software binaries and recreate their functionality, one software developer and student has created a project designed to make this process more difficult.

Timo Zhang's project is called Blind LLM Agents (BLA), and as its name suggests, it attempts to interfere with efforts by AI agents to scrutinize app code.

"Coding agents can reverse-engineer shipped packages, CLIs, and WASM in minutes," Zhang told The Register in an email. "Classic obfuscation was built for humans and static tools, not LLMs that reason about meaning. Blind LLM Agents is a protection layer for that threat model."

Such agents can also help developers build alternatives to existing commercial software.

Last month, Artcraft, a two-person development shop, released seven open-source apps that aim to be replacements for Adobe's commercial apps Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere Pro, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro. Artcraft claims these apps are "clean-room reimplementations" written from scratch in Rust using Anthropic Opus 5.5.

Setting aside the question of whether enlisting an AI model to reimplement an app really immunizes the creator from legal risk, those making apps face the possibility that someone will have an LLM probe published app binaries and reconstruct them through reverse engineering. There's in fact a framework for this, Reverse Engineer Anything (REA).

Zhang has faced some criticism on social media for creating a limited barrier to copying other people's work (which at this point might simply be the work of another LLM). But not everyone accepts that all publicly accessible binaries should be easily available for review and reuse. BLA cannot prevent committed reverse engineering efforts, but it may add a bit of friction to the process when LLMs are involved.

"It doesn't write app code — it hardens what you've already built," Zhang said. "A transform pipeline (plus MCP tools / an agent Skill) applies renaming, lane splitting, seed-derived string encryption, build polymorphism, WASM export renaming, decoys, self-seal integrity checks, and a coverage matrix that won't claim protection it can't prove. Behavior stays equivalent; recovery cost goes up."

Zhang said various evaluations like red teaming and CrackMe challenges to recover keys or flags from hardened artifacts show that BLA is effective.

"We also drive REA (a reverse-engineering agent) against those builds," he said. "Fail-to-break is the pass. CI tracks defense score, self-verifies integrity coverage, and checks functional equivalence. We raise the cost — we don't claim it is unbreakable."

The project website says as much, noting that it raises the effort for analysis and adds decoy code, but doesn't promise protection against traditional interactive reverse engineering tools like Ghidra or Frida.

Zhang said he's aware of other software projects that aim to interfere with AI, such as Poison Fountain for poisoning training data and Anubis for deterring bots and scraping. BLA, he said, is different. It's for hardening shipping code against reverse engineering and LLM-aided analysis. ®

#10001. Introducing OlmoEarth embeddings: Custom embedding exports from OlmoEarth Studio for downstream analysis

📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth | 📊 Documentation: https://docs.olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings | 💻 Learn more about OlmoEarth: https://allenai.org/olmoearth

OlmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models. The source code and model weights are publicly available alongside the research paper, so the community can inspect exactly how these embeddings are generated.

Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration. Locations with similar surface characteristics end up with similar vectors; locations that differ land far apart. OlmoEarth embeddings have shown strong performance in our own benchmarking and in independent evaluations. The exported Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) are lightweight and easy to share. Choose your area of interest, time range, encoder variant, resolution, and imagery sources via the Studio UI or API, and get back a COG you can use however you like. If your application requires higher performance, Studio also supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

Custom-computed embeddings are now available for users of OlmoEarth Studio. Reach out if you're interested in gaining access. Instructions for using the publicly available OlmoEarth models to compute your own embeddings are available here.

Global structure in OlmoEarth embeddings from seasonal Sentinel-2 imagery across 1.1M samples. Colors indicate 15 k-means clusters in a PCA-reduced embedding space.

Computing embeddings follows the same workflow as any other prediction in Studio. First configure a model and run it, and then download the results. Several parameters tailor the output:

Different visualization options applied to the same embedding raster.

Studio delivers a COG with one band per embedding dimension. Vectors are stored as signed 8-bit integers (int8). Values range from -127 to +127, with -128 reserved for nodata. To recover floating-point vectors, see dequantize_embeddings in olmoearth_pretrain.

Because everything is computed on demand rather than pulled from a pre-computed global archive, your embeddings reflect exactly the conditions you care about. You can generate monthly embeddings to capture seasonal dynamics, not just annual snapshots.

The examples below all use OlmoEarth-v1-Tiny (192-dim) embeddings at 40-meter resolution with Sentinel-2 L2A composites (annual for most examples; monthly for change detection). Tiny is a lightweight encoder but still highly performant; for your own applications, you can swap it for a larger variant at the cost of higher compute and storage.

Pick a query pixel, extract its embedding, and compute cosine similarity against every other pixel. The result is a heatmap showing where the landscape looks most and least like your query pixel.

This query sits near the Merced urban center in California. Urban fabric and road corridors light up coherently while agricultural parcels stay dark. The model distinguishes built-up surfaces from cropland without any labels.

Switching the query to a small agricultural window, we define the query vector as the mean of the embedding vectors over that window, then pull Sentinel-2 imagery at the highest- and lowest-similarity locations to see what the model treats as similar and dissimilar.

The most similar patches (0.89 and above) are all agricultural parcels with irrigated fields. The least similar (around zero) are an airport with surrounding bare ground, a reservoir with dry terrain, and arid rangeland. No training data, no labels, just a dot product in embedding space.

Similarity search tells you "where is it like this?" but sometimes you need discrete labels across a region. Because the representations are already rich, a simple linear classifier can produce a wall-to-wall land-cover map from very few labeled pixels.

To test this, we labeled just 60 pixels (20 per class) over Ca Mau, Vietnam, a coastal mangrove region. Using ESA WorldCover 2021 as the label source for three classes (mangrove, water, other), we randomly sampled 20 pixels per class, trained a logistic regression with per-feature standardization, and predicted every pixel in the region.

From 60 labeled pixels, the classifier produces a coherent map with weighted F1 = 0.84. Mangrove stands, tidal channels, and open water are delineated across the entire region. The classifier saturates quickly: increasing from 30 to 300 labels barely changes accuracy, because the embeddings are doing most of the heavy lifting.

The core of the analysis is a few lines of Python:

This is a linear probe, a standard evaluation for foundation models. The fact that a logistic regression over 192 dimensions recovers land-cover boundaries from so few labels means the Tiny encoder has organized these ecological distinctions during pretraining. Larger variants (Base, 768-dim) encode even richer representations.

If you have ground-truth polygons, field survey points, or a coarse existing map, you can train a similar classifier and produce a wall-to-wall map for your own region of interest.

Because Studio can generate embeddings at any temporal resolution (monthly through annual), you can compare two time periods directly to identify where surface conditions have changed. Below, we computed monthly Sentinel-2 embeddings for the same region in September 2023 and September 2024 and measured per-pixel cosine distance. The Park Fire (July-September 2024) burn scar in Butte County, California lights up immediately.

No labels or training required—just two embedding COGs and a few lines of Python.

Sometimes you have no query location or reference labels. You just want to understand what structure exists in the embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a clean way to do this: reduce to three dimensions, map to R/G/B, and display as a false-color image. Similar embeddings get similar colors automatically.

Flevoland, in the Netherlands, is a reclaimed polder landscape with a regular grid of agricultural parcels. The PCA false-color image reproduces those boundaries with high fidelity. Different crop types, water bodies, and urban areas each get distinct hues. The embedding has internalized landscape structure without ever being told what a parcel or crop is.

This kind of unsupervised view is a quick way to see what structure the model has picked up across your area of interest.

Similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA exploration are simple operations on standard raster data that run in seconds. The power comes from the embeddings: learned representations that compress earth observation data into vectors capturing rich information about each location from many sensors and millions of training examples.

Custom embedding exports are available now. Create a project, configure an embeddings model, and compute your embeddings. The exported GeoTIFF works with any geospatial tool: QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, or your own scripts. For end-to-end code reproducing the examples in this post, see the embeddings tutorial, which includes working code for similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA visualization. To get hands-on without any local setup, try the Colab notebook.

The examples in this post all use frozen embeddings with no task-specific training. Embeddings are a great entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they enable fast, cost-effective generation of results, work well in resource-constrained environments, and are easy to share. For applications that require higher performance, OlmoEarth Studio also supports SFT, training a task-specific model head on your own labels, which typically outperforms linear probes on frozen features.

While we are always working to improve our pretraining approaches, it's important to check the quality of the embeddings for your use case using some of the techniques described above. Performance also depends on the quality of the input imagery—persistent cloud cover, atmospheric artifacts, or missing observations in the composite period can affect the resulting vectors.

Sentinel-2 L2A imagery from the European Space Agency, accessed via Microsoft Planetary Computer. ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 for mangrove reference. The global clustering visualization uses OlmoEarth-v1-Base (768-dim) with seasonal Sentinel-2 composites at patch size 8, instance-level embeddings over 1.1M pretraining samples.

#10000. US Government Email Systems Open to Abuse Thanks to Typos

Erroneous or outdated DNS records can give attackers surprising powers over organizations' email systems.

Simple oversights in domain name system (DNS) records are exposing government organizations to all kinds of potential impersonation, spying, and more.

In a new study of more than 25,000 government-related domains, SH Consulting founder Alex Shakhov found dozens whose DNS records referenced either mistyped, expired, or otherwise repurposed domains. Though few in number, those vulnerable included all sorts of agencies representing US towns, cities, counties, regulatory boards, and more.

Many of the erroneous records pointed to domains that were either available to, or already snapped up by, attackers. Depending on the nature of the error, they could allow attackers to send or receive email on behalf of vulnerable government agencies, reconfigure their DNS records, read their security records, and more.

"Typos in DNS are very dangerous, because technically the organization is being hacked without anyone breaking into its systems," Shakhov tells Dark Reading. "You already have a domain with a reputation established over years. You put whatever IPs you want into DNS, spin up an email server, and send emails out, exploiting that reputation and users' trust. And these attacks are very difficult to detect, because the attackers didn't break anything. They just registered a domain sitting in the DNS that nobody knew existed."

Related:Japan Pushes Emergency Funding for Cybersecurity as AI-Assisted Breaches Rise

After Dark Reading ran this story, Livingston County, Mich., the city of Waynesboro, Tenn., and the Alabama legislature have all implemented or begun working on fixes for their DNS vulnerabilities.

Little matters more to a website's security than its DNS records, which include instructions about where the website lives in IP space (A/AAAA), its domain (CNAME), how its email is handled (MX, TXT), and who decides these details in the first place (NS). At the end of the day, though, it's a totally public set of information in plaintext. A simple typo in any of these instructions can have surprisingly significant impacts.

Take Livingston County, Mich., and the city of Pikeville, Ky. These two government bodies seem to have authorized Amazon's Simple Email Service (SES) for its day-to-day email needs and, as such, their TXT records specify it as a trusted third-party provider. The domains they list, however, contain typos: "amzonses[.]com" and "amasonses[.]com." Thanks to these mistakes, these bodies have been allowing a non-Amazon entity to send emails on their behalf.

To what end? When Shakhov checked the two organizations' Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allowlists, he found that Pikeville's listed 75 IP addresses, and Livingston's listed more than 32,000 different IP addresses, all authorized to send mail on behalf of their official domains. As a result, Pikeville's official government domain is now listed on the URI blacklist website "URIBL," and Shakhov assessed that "it's reasonable to assume the domain is still being used for abuse."

Related:Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

In the Livingston County case, the "included" SPF list was rotated every three to eight days since 2021. This suggested that an attacker was performing a "snowshoe" operation: switching to new sending IPs, sending unwanted or malicious emails, and once those IPs attained bad reputations, cycling in new ones.

This information alone doesn't necessarily prove that attackers were abusing Livingston County's email domain, or prove how much they might have. But it does prove that they could have. Shakhov connected the actor behind this compromise to a previously documented group that was seen abusing websites from major corporations such as Oracle and CNN Money as well as universities — like the Universities of California in Los Angeles, Davis, San Diego, and Santa Cruz (UCLA, UC Davis, UC San Diego, and UC Santa Cruz) — and the Connecticut state government, thanks to expired CNAME records.

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

Just about any DNS record can be abused if it contains a typo or refers to an otherwise incorrect domain for some other reason. The nature of the abuse depends, however, on the record in question. Once they register a so-called "dangling" (purchasable) domain, attackers can intercept mail (if the issue lies with an MX record), serve spam content (if it's in CNAME or NS), send phishing that appears to come from a legitimate sender (SPF), or collect security intel through Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC).

For example, the website for the City of Rupert, Idaho, currently refers to its neighbor Heyburn's old domain name, heyburnidaho[.]org. That domain was purchased by a malicious actor, which reworked its name server (NS) records to point to its shady gambling website. The actor also arranged to be able to send and receive emails from addresses with an @heyburnidaho.org suffix.

A less serious exposure could occur if attackers grab hold of a DMARC reporting domain. DMARC is an email security protocol, and its part of a TXT record can tell a mail server where to send reports. Those reports can contain sensitive information about an organization's email infrastructure. Shakhov found 11 local government institutions at risk of this sort of information theft, including four county and law enforcement agencies from Jennings County, Ind.

Taking advantage of these situations is one of the easiest jobs hackers can choose for themselves. "Attackers constantly scan DNS records for vulnerabilities and mistyped domains, because it's one of the easiest and cheapest ways to get into someone's infrastructure," Shakhov explains.

"Records at the root domain, like MX, NS, SPF, DMARC, CAA, etc., can be looked up by anyone," he continues. "Subdomains are harder to find, but Certificate Transparency logs reveal most of them. So attackers just scan DNS in bulk and get whatever they want. It's even easier for government domains, because it’s only about 26,000 domains to scan, and attackers can do it multiple times a day at almost no cost. CISA even publishes the full list of .gov domains, so attackers don't have to find them."

Shakhov laments that while DNS has been around for nearly half a century, "There's typically no one at an organization responsible for DNS management. As a result, over time it often turns into a graveyard of expired domains from previous vendors, former corporate domains forgotten after acquisitions and mergers, or just typos, when someone typed a record by hand instead of copying and pasting it."

Proper DNS hygiene, he says, requires that organizations follow at least a few core processes. First of all, he argues, "Admins and IT teams must stop typing DNS records by hand. Across millions of domains we scanned this year, 47% of the unregistered domains we found in SPF and DMARC records were typos, either of the organization's own domain or of a provider's."

Second, organizations must have a map of their DNS infrastructure and know where every DNS record came from. Depending on the circumstances, this can be easier said than done. "At universities, it's quite common for students to put a project on GitHub and ask the IT team to add a CNAME so it lives under the university domain," Shakhov explains. "The student graduates, but the CNAME stays. The GitHub account gets abandoned and removed, so whoever creates an account with the same name already has a CNAME sitting under the university's DNS."

Organizations should also consider registering misspelled versions of their own domains to prevent attackers from snapping them up later.

And, finally, "Regular DNS audits are a must," Shakhov says. "In most cases, it's just a simple script that scans your DNS for invalid domains or destinations and flags them. It's never been that difficult to do a quarterly DNS review to make sure everything is up to date."

This story was updated at 3:05 p.m. ET on Nov. 10 to reflect actions by multiple US government agencies to address their DNS vulnerabilities.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.
